what: Raymond Goertz at Argonne National Laboratory built and patented a bilateral master-slave manipulator for handling radioactive material through a hot-cell window.

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: In 1949, while working for the Atomic Energy Commission at Argonne National Laboratory, Goertz filed a patent for an early master-slave manipulator

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: The initial master-slave manipulator device was designed by Goertz in 1948 as a seven-degree-of-freedom bilateral (symmetrical) metal tape transmission pantograph device

note: Design dated 1948, patent filed 1949; no fetched page gives the date of the first working demonstration. Earlier Torres Quevedo Telekino (1903) was remote control without the operator seeing or feeling through the machine; rejected. GE/Payne 1948 device not verified.

what: Modified Goertz master-slave manipulator (CRL Model 8) went into commercial production for nuclear remote handling.

sources.title: Raymond Goertz
sources.quote: by 1954 a modified version of the master-slave manipulator (CRL Model 8) began commercial production

note: Argonne likely used earlier models in hot cells from about 1949-51 but no fetched source dates that; 1954 is a later bound only.

what: Luna 1 (USSR), launched 2 Jan 1959, left Earth orbit, passed the Moon and became the first spacecraft in solar orbit, returning data.

sources.title: Luna 1
sources.quote: was the first spacecraft to reach the vicinity of Earth's Moon, the first spacecraft to leave Earth's orbit

note: Considered Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 (Earth-orbit satellites, not another body or deep space) and rejected them. Earlier Pioneer 0/1 attempts failed. Deep-sea robot probes not found in fetchable sources.

what: Luna 3 (USSR) photographed the far side of the Moon and radioed the pictures to Earth; Luna 2 had impacted the Moon in Sept 1959.

sources.title: Luna 3
sources.quote: It was the first mission to photograph the far side of the Moon and the third Soviet space probe to be sent to the neighborhood of the Moon.

note: Exploration return (images) is the real purpose. Luna 2 impact (1959-09-13) also reported data but is a hard landing. Lunokhod 1 (1970) is the first rover, later than these.

what: Stoddart's rotaxane molecular shuttle, the breakthrough in synthesising artificial molecular machines (first reported working example 1994 in same article).

sources.title: Molecular machine
sources.quote: the actual breakthrough in practical approaches to synthesize artificial molecular machines (AMMs) took place in 1991 with the invention of a "molecular shuttle"

note: Molecular-scale machine only; no robot working inside the body exists, so no first_practical_use or mass_adoption. Sauvage catenane 1983 considered, a structure not a machine. The first pass cited 2004-2010 DNA walkers, which are later.

what: Hideo Kodama (Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute) published methods and results for building 3D plastic models layer by layer from photo-hardening polymer.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: His research results as journal papers were published in April and November 1981.

sources.title: 3D printing
sources.quote: In April 1980, Hideo Kodama of Nagoya Municipal Industrial Research Institute invented two additive methods for fabricating three-dimensional plastic models

note: Earlier than Hull's 1984 patent. Raytheon 1982 layered-powder patent is later. Whether Kodama's design was driven by a digital design file is not stated; fit is on layer-by-layer automatic building.

what: 3D Systems, co-founded by Chuck Hull, commercialised stereolithography (first machine, SLA-1, reported 1987).

sources.title: Stereolithography
sources.quote: After the patent was granted in 1986, Hull co-founded the world's first 3D printing company, 3D Systems, to commercialize it.

note: Quote supports commercialisation after 1986 only; the 1987 SLA-1 date comes from the first pass and was not fetched. No mass_adoption established (consumer RepRap era 2005+ not sourced as routine use).

what: Francois Willeme's photosculpture: photographs taken in the round used to reproduce a person as a 3D sculpture.

sources.title: Photosculpture
sources.quote: The process was invented and patented by French artist (painter, sculptor and photographer) François Willème in 1860.

note: Records the full shape of an object for reproduction, but optically and not digitally. Ferranti's 1950s coordinate-measuring machine measures points only and is not for reproduction; Cyberware 1984 head scanner from first pass could not be sourced.

what: Lawrence Sperry demonstrated the Sperry gyroscopic autopilot in Paris (flying hands off the controls); system developed 1912.

sources.title: Autopilot
sources.quote: Lawrence Sperry, the son of famous inventor Elmer Sperry, demonstrated it in 1914 at an aviation safety contest held in Paris.

note: Development in 1912 considered; no dated demonstration found for 1912. Day 1914-06-18 comes from the first pass and was not confirmed.

what: Standard Oil tanker J.A. Moffet became the first ship to use an autopilot (Sperry gyropilot).

sources.title: Autopilot
sources.quote: In the early 1920s, the Standard Oil tanker J.A. Moffet became the first ship to use an autopilot.

note: Year 1922 is from memory of the Moffet installation; source says only early 1920s. Aircraft use: 1930 Army Air Corps three-hour test, 1947 full transatlantic autopilot flight, later than this.

what: Gemini 3 flew with the IBM Gemini guidance computer, controlling mission maneuvers (orbit changes by crew).

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

sources.title: Gemini 3
sources.quote: It was the first U.S. mission in which the crew fired thrusters to change the size and shape of their orbit

note: Earlier than the first pass (Apollo 1968). That Gemini 3 carried the computer is from background knowledge, not a fetched sentence. Missile and submarine inertial guidance computers (late 1950s) not checked.

what: Same flight: first operational use of an onboard computer for orbital maneuvers on a crewed spacecraft.

sources.title: Gemini Guidance Computer
sources.quote: The computer, which facilitated the control of mission maneuvers, was designed by the IBM Federal Systems Division.

note: Same event as the demonstration; see note there.

what: Tsukuba Mechanical Engineering Laboratory (Japan) vehicle drove itself at up to 30 km/h using two cameras to detect street markings.

sources.title: History of self-driving cars
sources.quote: In 1977, the first self-driving car that operated independently of wires under the road was designed by the Japanese Tsukuba Mechanical Engineering Laboratory.

note: 1950s wire-guided cars (RCA/GM) and 1920s radio-controlled cars considered; they follow buried wire or have a remote operator, so rejected. Dickmanns 1987 is later. No fully driverless public service verified (Waymo One Dec 2018 was remotely monitored), so no practical use.

what: A. M. Low's radio-controlled de Havilland monoplane flew under control in Britain.

sources.title: Unmanned aerial vehicle
sources.quote: Low confirmed that Geoffrey de Havilland's monoplane was the one that flew under control on 21 March 1917 using his radio system.

note: Hewitt-Sperry Automatic Airplane flew about 1,000 yards controlled on 1918-03-06 (Wikipedia: first unmanned heavier-than-air controlled flight); Low's claim is disputed and earlier than that. 1849 Austrian balloons are unpowered, rejected.

what: DJI Phantom, an affordable ready-to-fly consumer drone, launched in 2013 and opened the consumer drone market.

sources.title: Unmanned aerial vehicle
sources.quote: The DJI Phantom was considered one of the most influential consumer drone products ever made.

note: Year of launch of the product that started mass consumer use, not a measured usage figure. First practical use (1920s-30s target drones such as Fairey Queen, Queen Bee) not dated by a fetched source.

what: Skylab launched with an onboard digital computer controlling its attitude and pointing.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: The mission computer used aboard Skylab was the IBM System/4Pi TC-1, a relative of the AP-101 Space Shuttle computers.

sources.title: Skylab
sources.quote: Skylab was launched on May 14, 1973, by the modified Saturn V.

note: Sources show an onboard computer for attitude control only, not life support. Salyut 1 (1971) computers not found in fetchable sources, so an earlier event may exist.

what: UNIVAC I, used by CBS on election night, predicted an Eisenhower landslide from 5.5% of the vote.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: The fifth machine (built for the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission) was used by CBS to predict the result of the 1952 presidential election.

note: Earlier computer forecasts not found. Statistical model of people, as definition requires; the machine was off on the first try, but the 442 vs 438 electoral vote result was close.

what: Same broadcast: the forecast was used on live television for the real election.

sources.title: UNIVAC I
sources.quote: On election night, Eisenhower received 34,075,029 votes in a 442–89 Electoral College victory. UNIVAC had a margin of error of 3.5%

note: Same event as the demonstration. Computerized predictions then became a widely used part of election night broadcasts, but no dated source for mass adoption.

what: Chile's Project Cybersyn linked state enterprises by telex to a central mainframe for production monitoring and economic simulation.

sources.title: Project Cybersyn
sources.quote: Project Cybersyn was a Chilean economic project developed from 1971 to 1973 during the socialist presidency of Salvador Allende

note: Date 1972 is from the first pass (October 1972 strike); fetched page gives only 1971-73. USAF Project SCOOP (linear-programming planning on SEAC, about 1951) may be earlier but I could not fetch a source. NYSE DOT (1970s) only routes orders.

concept_note: No milestone. The JPL STAR (Self-Testing And Repairing) computer, breadboard running a program in March 1969 (search snippet), is the likely first demonstration, but I could not fetch a page to quote, so it is dropped. SAPO (1951) used voting to mask faults but did not repair itself.
Kept Goertz master-slave manipulator (1948-49) but low confidence on demonstration date; added 1954 commercial production as practical use. No mass adoption: not routine for ordinary people.
Moved earlier than first pass (Lunokhod 1970): Luna 1 (1959) and Luna 3 (1959) fit the definition. No mass adoption; not applicable.
Earlier than first pass: artificial molecular machine (Stoddart shuttle) 1991. Nothing has worked inside the body, so no practical use or mass adoption.
Kodama (1981) predates Hull (1984). Practical use 1987 is low confidence. No mass adoption established.
Photosculpture 1860 is the earliest fit (analogue). First-pass Cyberware 1984 could not be sourced. No practical use or mass adoption sourced.
Kept 1914 demonstration; added ship autopilot as earliest practical use (about 1922). No mass adoption date found.
Moved earlier than first pass (Apollo 1968) to Gemini 3, 1965, at low confidence. No mass adoption.
Moved earlier than first pass (1987) to Tsukuba 1977. No practical use: no fully unsupervised public service verified. No mass adoption.
Moved earlier than first pass: Low 1917 (disputed) versus Hewitt-Sperry 1918. Added consumer-drone year 2013 for mass adoption. Practical use not dated.
Only candidate found: Skylab 1973 with an onboard computer. Fit to life-support control not shown, so confidence low. No practical use or mass adoption separate from this.
Never real: no state or city has been governed by a central computer. No milestones.
UNIVAC election forecast 1952 kept as demonstration and practical use. Psychohistory never real. No mass adoption date.
Cybersyn 1972 kept as low-confidence practical use; algorithmic trading and SCOOP not sourced, so no other milestones.

No milestone. Fair Isaac founded 1956 (fetched) but I could not confirm that 1958 credit scoring ran on a computer; Nielsen computer processing of ratings reported from 1959 in a search snippet, page not fetchable. Dropped for lack of a fetched source.
